passage: Asif had a sheet of paper folded in his pocket: a plan for a two-year design course, the fees, and a list of jobs it could lead to. All week he had rehearsed at the dining table, but each time Ammi mentioned the neighbour's son at the engineering college, his words dried up. He felt the weight of his father's overtime too. On Sunday his cousin Karthik said, "If you defy them or just go along, you'll resent both. Show them the plan." That evening Asif put the paper on the table. "Abba, Ammi, I know what you have given up for my studies. I want to try design, and here is how I would pay, and what I would do if it hasn't worked by the end of the first year." His father read it twice. "Ask me again tomorrow," he said. It wasn't yes. But Ammi refilled Asif's plate.

qa.q: What did Asif carry folded in his pocket?
qa.a: He carried a plan for a two-year design course, with the fees and a list of jobs.

qa.q: What was Asif feeling as he rehearsed at the dining table?
qa.a: He was torn and guilty; his words dried up because he felt the weight of his father's overtime and the family's expectations.
It offered a third route between defying and going along: an honest, respectful conversation with a concrete plan.

qa.q: How might Asif's father have felt while reading the plan?
qa.a: He was probably surprised and worried but respectful of the effort, since he read it twice and asked for a day, which suggests he was taking it seriously.

grounding: A young adult torn between own aspiration and family expectation has an honest, respectful talk with a concrete plan.

subtopic: Parents pressure on career or marriage
passage:
"Sharma Aunty has a boy for you. Just meet him this Sunday," Mummy said, passing the dal.

Aadhya put her spoon down. "Mummy, I don't want to meet anyone before my thesis is done."

"Everyone your age is getting settled," Papa said. "We won't be here forever."

"I know." Aadhya's throat tightened. "You've done everything for me. That's why this is hard. If I say no, I feel like a bad daughter. If I say yes, I feel like I'm lying to myself."

Mummy's face softened a little. "So what do you want?"

"Here's my plan. Dolma ma'am says my thesis will be submitted by June. After that I'll start meeting people, and I'll tell you honestly what I think each time. Till June, please no meetings."

Papa looked at Mummy. "June," he said. "And you'll really meet them?"

"I promise. And I'll call Sharma Aunty myself to say thank you."

qa.q: By when does Dolma ma'am say the thesis will be submitted?
qa.a: Dolma ma'am says the thesis will be submitted by June.

qa.q: What was Aadhya feeling when her throat tightened?
qa.a: Aadhya felt torn and guilty, caught between love and duty to her parents and her own wish to finish her thesis first.

qa.q: Why did Aadhya's approach work better than refusing outright or agreeing out of fear?
qa.a: She thanked her parents, named her feelings honestly and offered a concrete plan with a date, which they could accept.

qa.q: How does Papa seem to see Aadhya's plan?
qa.a: Papa seems cautious but willing, needing to hear that Aadhya will really meet people after June before he agrees.

grounding: Shows a young woman torn between family marriage expectations and her own goals, who has an honest, respectful talk with a concrete plan.

passage:
The week after Papa's knee operation, everyone said the same thing: "Now Lokesh will run the shop."

I'm Lokesh, and I was in the final year of architecture in Nagpur. I loved it. But every time I looked at Papa's bandaged leg, I felt like a selfish person for even wanting to go back.

For a few days I did nothing. I didn't answer my classmates and I didn't tell my parents what I was thinking. My elder sister Seema noticed. "You're sulking in the hardware aisle," she said. "Talk to them."

So one evening I sat with both of them and said it straight: "I'm grateful for this shop. It paid for my studies. I want to finish my degree. Here's what I can do: come home every weekend, train Raju bhaiya to handle the counter, and check the stock lists every Sunday."

Papa was quiet for a long time. Then he said, "Show me the schedule."

qa.a: Lokesh was in the final year of architecture in Nagpur.

qa.q: What was Lokesh feeling in the days after Papa's operation?
qa.a: Lokesh felt guilty and torn, like a selfish person for wanting to go back to studies while Papa was hurt.

qa.q: What did Lokesh do that turned the situation around?
qa.a: Lokesh stopped avoiding it, thanked the parents honestly and offered a concrete plan: weekends at home, training Raju bhaiya and Sunday stock checks.

qa.q: How does Seema see Lokesh during those first few days?
qa.a: Seema sees Lokesh sulking and stuck, and believes an honest talk with the parents is the way out.

grounding: Shows a young person torn between family duty and own aspirations who has an honest, respectful conversation with a concrete plan.
